A carer is a person who looks after someone who cannot fully look after themselves. The person being looked after usually needs help because of old age, illness, disability, or a mental health condition. A carer steps in to provide that help — either as a job or simply out of love and duty.

Think of it this way: if someone in your life suddenly became very ill and could no longer cook, wash, move around, or take their medication alone, and you began doing those things for them regularly — you would be their carer.
What Does a Carer Actually Do?

A carer's responsibilities can be wide-ranging. They might:

  • Help someone wash, dress, and groom themselves
  • Prepare and serve meals
  • Give or manage medication
  • Help the person move around safely
  • Take them to medical appointments
  • Handle household tasks like cleaning and laundry
  • Provide emotional support and companionship
  • In serious cases, make decisions on the person's behalf

The level of care depends entirely on how much help the person needs. Some carers help for a few hours a week; others are available around the clock.
Two Main Types of Carers

1. Informal (unpaid) carers
These are family members, friends, or neighbours who look after a loved one without being paid. This is the most common type. A wife caring for her husband who has dementia, a parent caring for a child with a severe disability, or an adult child looking after an elderly parent — all of these people are informal carers. They did not choose this role as a career; life brought it to them.

2. Formal (paid) carers
These are people employed specifically to provide care. They may work in care homes, hospitals, or visit people in their own homes. This is their profession. Sometimes called care workers, they are trained to handle medical, personal, and emotional needs.
Who Do Carers Look After?

A carer can look after anyone who is vulnerable or dependent, including:

  • Elderly people who are frail or have conditions like dementia or Alzheimer's
  • People with physical disabilities who need help with movement or daily tasks
  • People with learning disabilities who need support with understanding or managing everyday life
  • People with serious illnesses such as cancer, multiple sclerosis, or heart disease
  • People with mental health conditions who struggle to manage daily life independently
  • Children with complex needs
An Important Nuance: Carer vs. A "Caring Person"

These two things sound similar but mean very different things.

  • A caring person is simply someone who is kind, warm, and considerate in their personality. It describes a character trait.
  • A carer is a specific role. It describes what someone does — the active, ongoing responsibility of looking after a dependent person.

You can be a caring person without ever being a carer. And a carer, by definition, is performing a real, practical function — not just being emotionally supportive in general.
"Carer" vs. "Caregiver" — A Regional Difference

This is worth knowing. "Carer" is the standard word used in British English — in the UK, Australia, New Zealand, and other countries that follow British usage. "Caregiver" is the preferred word in American English. Both words mean exactly the same thing. If you are reading a British article or speaking in a British context, you will see "carer." If you are reading something American, you will see "caregiver."
Special Categories of Carers

Young carers — Children or teenagers who take on caring responsibilities for a parent, sibling, or relative. This is a significant and often overlooked group, as the weight of caring can affect their education, social life, and wellbeing.

Primary carer — When more than one person shares caring duties, the primary carer is the main person who carries the greatest share of responsibility.
The Human Reality of Being a Carer

Being a carer — especially an unpaid one — can be deeply rewarding but also exhausting and emotionally demanding. Many carers experience what is known as "carer burnout": a state of physical and emotional exhaustion that comes from giving so much of themselves over a long period. Because of this, many countries have specific support systems for carers, including financial assistance (such as Carer's Allowance in the UK), legal rights, and access to respite care — which means temporary relief so the carer can rest.
Example Sentences

• "My aunt has been my grandfather's carer for the past three years since he had his stroke."
  • "She works as a paid carer at a residential home for people with learning disabilities."
  • "The government introduced new policies to support unpaid carers who often sacrifice their own careers."
  • "He became a young carer at the age of twelve when his mother was diagnosed with MS."
  • "The hospital arranged for a professional carer to visit her at home twice a day."
Summary

A carer is someone — paid or unpaid — who regularly looks after another person who needs help due to illness, disability, old age, or a mental health condition. The role involves practical tasks, emotional support, and often great personal sacrifice. The word is standard in British English; Americans use caregiver instead. Carers can be family members thrust into the role by circumstance, professionals doing it as a career, or even children carrying responsibilities far beyond their years.
